subtype: Approach: testing with one paying client [Action]
passage:
Wei had a folder of class projects and no idea what anyone would pay for them. So before building a website, she walked into the bakery on her street in Toronto and asked the owner, Diego, whether he needed a poster for his weekend bread sale. They agreed on forty dollars.
She started a timer on her laptop. The layout took ninety minutes, far longer than she'd guessed. Then Diego asked for bigger prices, a photo of the rye loaf, and the Spanish word for 'fresh' in one corner. After three rounds of changes, the timer said four and a half hours.
That night she wrote down everything he had asked for, in order. Next time she would ask those questions first. The poster went up on Friday, and on Monday Diego asked for a second one for December.

qa.q: How long had the poster taken by the end, according to the timer?
What was Wei feeling when the timer showed four and a half hours?
qa.a: Probably surprised and a bit deflated that forty dollars covered so much work, yet steady enough to turn it into a list of lessons.

qa.q: What would Wei change first before taking a second poster job?
qa.a: Ask Diego's kinds of questions about prices, photos and wording at the start, and check whether the price still matches the real hours.

qa.q: How does the test look from Diego's side?
qa.a: For Diego it is a cheap way to get a good poster shaped by his own requests, and he is pleased enough to order another. 🙂

grounding: Shows a student designing one poster for one local shop at a modest price, timing it and learning what the customer asks before advertising.

subtype: Approach: testing with one paying client [Action]
passage:
The photocopy shop by the college library was always crowded at ten. Ankita waited until the queue thinned, then showed Leela, who ran the counter, three poster sketches for the new spiral-binding service. 'Five hundred rupees for one final poster,' Ankita said. 'I want to see how many hours one poster really eats up.'
Leela picked the blue sketch. Ankita wrote the time in her notebook: 11:05.
By Thursday she had a draft. Leela read it aloud to two students at the counter. One asked, 'Is it same-day?' The other asked, 'How much for twenty pages?' Neither answer was on the poster.
Ankita added both, printed it on the shop's own machine, and closed her notebook entry: nearly six hours over three days, two things customers really ask. Only then did she think about pinning her name on the college notice board.

qa.q: What two questions did the students at the counter ask?
qa.a: 'Is it same-day?' and 'How much for twenty pages?'

qa.q: Why did Ankita want to time the first poster?
qa.a: She was unsure how long design work really takes and felt cautious about advertising herself before she knew.

qa.q: What else could Ankita test before putting her name on the notice board?
qa.a: She could make one poster for a college club or another campus stall, to see whether the hours and the customer questions come out similar.

qa.q: How does the poster project look to Leela?
qa.a: Leela gets a poster that answers what her customers actually ask, from a student who listened before selling.

grounding: Shows a student making one paid poster for one campus shop, timing the work and learning customers' real questions before promoting herself.
